clinicalPearls: Nephrocalcinosis is generalised deposition of calcium salts within the renal parenchyma, distinct from discrete calculi in the collecting system
The medullary pattern is far more common and usually reflects a disorder of calcium handling
The classic medullary causes are hyperparathyroidism, distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis and medullary sponge kidney
Further medullary causes include hypervitaminosis D, sarcoidosis, milk-alkali syndrome and primary hyperoxaluria
Cortical nephrocalcinosis is rarer and follows acute cortical necrosis, chronic glomerulonephritis or severe pyelonephritis
It is often found incidentally on imaging; ultrasound shows echogenic medullary pyramids in the medullary pattern
Management is directed at the underlying metabolic cause rather than at the calcification itself
Distal renal tubular acidosis is suggested when nephrocalcinosis accompanies a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine, and is treated with alkali replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Nephrocalcinosis denotes deposition of calcium, as oxalate or phosphate, diffusely through the renal tissue, most often in the medulla. Medullary deposition arises when there is an increased filtered calcium load, impaired urinary acidification or reduced inhibitor activity, as in hyperparathyroidism, distal renal tubular acidosis (where alkaline urine and hypocitraturia favour calcium phosphate precipitation), medullary sponge kidney with stasis in dilated collecting ducts, and states of hypercalcaemia or hyperoxaluria. Cortical nephrocalcinosis instead follows destructive processes such as acute cortical necrosis or chronic infection, where calcium is laid down in devitalised tissue as dystrophic calcification.
additionalDifferentials: Primary hyperparathyroidism and other hypercalcaemic states
Acute cortical necrosis or chronic pyelonephritis for the cortical pattern
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound, supplemented by CT, to confirm and characterise a medullary versus cortical pattern
Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone
Serum and urine pH, bicarbonate and electrolytes to assess for distal renal tubular acidosis
Serum vitamin D and, where indicated, angiotensin-converting enzyme for sarcoidosis
redFlags: Progressive chronic kidney disease from an untreated underlying disorder
Severe hypercalcaemia with acute kidney injury
Nephrocalcinosis in a child suggesting primary hyperoxaluria or an inherited tubulopathy
reference.prognosis: The renal outlook depends on the underlying cause and how early it is treated; some tubulopathies stabilise with alkali therapy, whereas primary hyperoxaluria and progressive hypercalcaemic disorders can lead to established renal failure.
pitfalls: Confusing nephrocalcinosis, which is parenchymal, with nephrolithiasis in the collecting system
Failing to search for a treatable metabolic cause such as distal renal tubular acidosis or hyperparathyroidism
Missing primary hyperoxaluria in a child, in whom it is progressive and serious
Attributing renal impairment to the calcification rather than the underlying disease
